claim: In budding yeast, if the spindle becomes mispositioned, cells prevent exit from mitosis by inhibiting the mitotic exit network (MEN).
source: In budding yeast, if the spindle becomes mispositioned, cells prevent exit from mitosis by inhibiting the mitotic exit network (MEN).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known mechanism and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The MEN is a signaling cascade that localizes to spindle pole bodies (SPBs) and activates the phosphatase Cdc14.
source: The MEN is a signaling cascade that localizes to spindle pole bodies (SPBs) and activates the phosphatase Cdc14.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and elaborated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Eliminating cMT–bud neck interactions does not trigger exit from mitosis.
source: Here we find that 1) eliminating cMT– bud neck interactions does not trigger exit from mitosis
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Loss of cMT-bud neck interactions does not precede Cdc14 activation.
source: 2) loss of these interactions does not precede Cdc14 activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Exit from mitosis occurs when one SPB enters the bud despite the presence of a mispositioned spindle.
source: Furthermore, using binucleate cells, we show that exit from mitosis occurs when one SPB enters the bud despite the presence of a mispositioned spindle.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: Exit from mitosis is triggered by a correctly positioned spindle rather than inhibited by improper spindle position.
source: We conclude that exit from mitosis is triggered by a correctly positioned spindle rather than inhibited by improper spindle position.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the site of cytokinesis forms independently of mitotic spindle position.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, coupling exit from mitosis with spindle position is particularly important because the site of cytokinesis forms independently of mitotic spindle position (Pruyne et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Budding yeast has evolved mechanisms that align the spindle and ensure that cytokinesis only occurs after the nucleus has been partitioned between the mother cell and bud.
source: Thus budding yeast has evolved mechanisms that align the spindle and that ensure that cytokinesis only occurs after the nucleus has been partitioned between the mother cell and bud, the future daughter cell (Bardin et al., 2000; Miller et al., 1999; Pereira et al., 2000; Yeh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Budding yeast employs two redundant mechanisms to position the spindle along the mother–bud axis.
source: Budding yeast employs two redundant mechanisms to position the spindle along the mother – bud axis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and elaborated with details about the Kar9 and dynein pathways.

claim: The first positioning mechanism relies on the type V myosin motor Myo2, which together with its adaptor Kar9 and the plus-end microtubule binding protein Bim1, positions the pre-anaphase spindle at the bud neck by pulling cytoplasmic microtubules along actin cables.
source: The first positioning mechanism relies on the type V myosin motor Myo2. Myo2, together with its adaptor Kar9 and the plus-end microtubule binding protein Bim1, positions the pre-anaphase spindle at the bud neck by pulling cytoplasmic microtubules (cMTs) along actin cables (Beach et al., 2000; Kopecká and Gabriel, 1998; Miller et al., 1999; Miller and Rose, 1998; Palmer et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The second spindle positioning pathway is active during anaphase and requires the minus-end microtubule motor protein dynein, together with its associated coactivating complex dynactin.
source: The second pathway is active during anaphase and requires the minus-end microtubule motor protein dynein, together with its associated coactivating complex dynactin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Dynein, when anchored to the cell cortex by Num1, aligns the spindle by essentially towing it along the cortex of the cell.
source: Dynein, when anchored to the cell cortex by Num1, aligns the spindle by essentially towing it along the cortex of the cell (Farkasovsky and Küntzel, 2001; Heil-Chapdelaine et al., 2000; Muhua et al., 1994; Yeh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cells lacking both spindle positioning pathways are inviable.
source: The consequences of eliminating either positioning pathway are minor but cells lacking both pathways are inviable (Miller and Rose, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cells that fail to segregate the nucleus into the bud will arrest in late anaphase with the spindle mispositioned in the mother cell compartment.
source: Cells that fail to segregate the nucleus into the bud will arrest in late anaphase with the spindle mispositioned in the mother cell compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: If the cell manages to correct the positioning defect and threads the nucleus through the bud neck into the bud, it will then disassemble the anaphase spindle and exit from mitosis.
source: If the cell manages to correct this positioning defect and threads the nucleus through the bud neck into the bud, it will then disassemble the anaphase spindle and exit from mitosis (Yeh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Yeast cells link spindle position and exit from mitosis through the regulation of the essential phosphatase Cdc14.
source: Yeast cells link spindle position and exit from mitosis through the regulation of the essential phosphatase Cdc14 (Bardin et al., 2000; D'Aquino et al., 2005; Pereira et al., 2000; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cdc14 functions to reverse mitotic cyclin-CDK activity by dephosphorylating cyclin-CDK targets as well as by targeting cyclins for degradation.
source: Cdc14 functions to reverse mitotic cyclin-CDK (cyclin dependent kinase) activity by dephosphorylating cyclin-CDK targets as well as by targeting cyclins for degradation (Jaspersen et al., 1998; Visintin et al., 1998; Zachariae et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cdc14 functions cause exit from mitosis, the final cell cycle transition that encompasses disassembly of the mitotic spindle and cytokinesis.
source: These Cdc14 functions cause exit from mitosis, the final cell cycle transition that encompasses disassembly of the mitotic spindle and cytokinesis (Stegmeier and Amon, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cdc14 is kept inactive from G1 to metaphase by its inhibitor Cfi1/Net1, which functions by sequestering the phosphatase in the nucleolus.
source: Cdc14 is kept inactive from G1 to metaphase by its inhibitor Cfi1/Net1, which functions by sequestering the phosphatase in the nucleolus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Upon anaphase entry, Cdc14 is released from Cfi1/Net1 to spread throughout the cell where it antagonizes mitotic CDK activity and returns the cell to G1.
source: It is only upon anaphase entry that Cdc14 is released from Cfi1/Net1 to spread throughout the cell where it antagonizes mitotic CDK activity and so returns the cell to G1 (Shou et al., 1999; Visintin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Two pathways control the activity of Cdc14: the Cdc14 early anaphase release network (FEAR) and the mitotic exit network (MEN).
source: Two pathways control the activity of Cdc14: the Cdc14 early anaphase release network (FEAR) and the mitotic exit network (MEN).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: The FEAR network serves to ensure anaphase spindle stability, spindle midzone assembly and proper rDNA segregation by transiently releasing Cdc14 from its inhibitor in the nucleolus during early anaphase.
source: The FEAR network serves to ensure anaphase spindle stability, spindle midzone assembly and proper rDNA segregation by transiently releasing Cdc14 from its inhibitor in the nucleolus during early anaphase (reviewed in Rock and Amon [2009]).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The MEN is responsible for sustained Cdc14 release during later stages of anaphase and is essential for cells to exit from mitosis.
source: In contrast, the MEN is responsible for sustained Cdc14 release during later stages of anaphase and is essential for cells to exit from mitosis (Jaspersen et al., 1998; Lee et al., 2001; Stegmeier et al., 2002; Visintin et al., 1998; 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The MEN is a GTPase signaling pathway whose constituents primarily localize to spindle pole bodies.
source: The MEN is a GTPase signaling pathway whose constituents primarily localize to spindle pole bodies (SPBs; yeast centrosomes).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: When Tem1 is in its GTP-bound state, the MEN is active and cells will exit from mitosis.
source: When Tem1 is in its GTP-bound state, the MEN is active and cells will exit from mitosis (Scarfone and Piatti, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: When Tem1 is inactive, the MEN is off and cells will arrest in anaphase.
source: Likewise when Tem1 is inactive, the MEN is off and cells will arrest in anaphase (Geymonat et al., 2002; Shirayama et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Tem1 regulates a kinase cascade comprised of the PAK-like kinase Cdc15 and the protein kinase Dbf2.
source: Tem1 regulates a kinase cascade comprised of the PAK-like kinase Cdc15 and the protein kinase Dbf2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Tem1 activates Cdc15 by recruiting it to the spindle pole body.
source: Tem1 activates Cdc15 by recruiting it to the spindle pole body (Rock and Amon, 2011; Visintin and Amon, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cdc15 recruits Dbf2 to spindle poles by creating a phospho-peptide binding domain on the SPB component and MEN scaffold Nud1.
source: Cdc15 in turn recruits Dbf2 to spindle poles by creating a phospho-peptide binding domain on the SPB component and MEN scaffold Nud1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In its phosphorylated state, Nud1 docks the Dbf2-activating subunit Mob1.
source: In its phosphorylated state, Nud1 docks the Dbf2-activating subunit Mob1 (Rock et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Activated Dbf2-Mob1 together with Cdc5 promote the sustained release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus through a largely uncharacterized mechanism.
source: Activated Dbf2-Mob1 together with Cdc5 then promote the sustained release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus through a largely uncharacterized mechanism (Manzoni et al., 2010; Mohl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Bub2/Bfa1 functions as a GTPase-activating protein complex (GAP) for Tem1 and inhibits the MEN.
source: Bub2/Bfa1 functions as a GTPase-activating protein complex (GAP) for Tem1 and so inhibits the MEN (Bloecher et al., 2000; Geymonat et al., 2002; Li, 1999; Shirayama et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The GAP complex is regulated by the protein kinase Kin4.
source: The GAP complex in turn is regulated by the protein kinase Kin4.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Kin4 localizes to the mother cell cortex as well as the mother cell-localized SPBs and functions to maintain GAP activity by preventing the inactivation of Bub2/Bfa1 by the Polo kinase Cdc5.
source: Kin4 localizes to the mother cell cortex as well as the mother cell-localized SPBs and functions to maintain GAP activity by preventing the inactivation of Bub2/Bfa1 by the Polo kinase Cdc5 (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lte1 localizes to the bud cell compartment and promotes exit from mitosis by preventing Kin4 localization to SPBs in the bud.
source: Lte1 localizes to the bud cell compartment and promotes exit from mitosis by preventing Kin4 localization to SPBs in the bud (Bertazzi et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lte1 displays homology with guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs).
source: Lte1 displays homology with guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs); however, whether Lte1 also functions as a GEF for Tem1 remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Whether Lte1 functions as a GEF for Tem1 remains unknown.
source: Lte1 displays homology with guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs); however, whether Lte1 also functions as a GEF for Tem1 remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Spindle position regulates MEN activity.
source: Spindle position regulates MEN activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: When the spindle is mispositioned, the MEN is inactive: Cdc14 is sequestered in the nucleolus and cells arrest in anaphase.
source: When the spindle is mispositioned, the MEN is inactive: Cdc14 is sequestered in the nucleolus and cells arrest in anaphase (Bardin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The regulatory mechanism that prevents exit from mitosis in response to spindle misposition is called the spindle position checkpoint (SPoC).
source: This regulatory mechanism that prevents exit from mitosis in response to spindle misposition is called the spindle position checkpoint (SPoC; [Muhua et al., 1998]).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The 'zone model' proposes that the cell is partitioned into a MEN inhibitory zone in the mother cell compartment and a MEN activating zone in the bud.
source: The 'zone model' proposes that the cell is partitioned into a MEN inhibitory zone in the mother cell compartment and a MEN activating zone in the bud (Figure 1A) (Chan and Amon, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The MEN inhibitor Kin4 localizes to the mother cell, the MEN activator Lte1 to the bud.
source: The MEN inhibitor Kin4 localizes to the mother cell, the MEN activator Lte1 to the bud (Bardin et al., 2000; D'Aquino et al., 2005; Pereira et al., 2000; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In the event that anaphase spindle elongation occurs only in the mother cell, the spindle poles cannot escape the negative regulation of Kin4 and the MEN is kept inactive.
source: In the event that anaphase spindle elongation occurs only in the mother cell, the spindle poles (where Tem1 resides) cannot escape the negative regulation of Kin4 and the MEN is kept inactive.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the zone model explanation.

claim: Inhibition of Tem1 is only relieved once the spindle realigns along the mother-bud axis and one spindle pole exits the Kin4 inhibitory zone.
source: Inhibition of Tem1 is only relieved once the spindle realigns along the mother-bud axis and one spindle pole exits the Kin4 inhibitory zone.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the zone model explanation.

claim: The bud compartment promotes Tem1 activation through redundant mechanisms: 1) the bud is largely devoid of Kin4 and 2) the Kin4 inhibitor Lte1 prevents any small amount of Kin4 present in the bud from localizing to the daughter SPB.
source: The bud compartment promotes Tem1 activation through redundant mechanisms: 1) the bud is largely devoid of Kin4 and 2) the Kin4 inhibitor Lte1 prevents any small amount of Kin4 present in the bud from localizing to the daughter SPB.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the zone model explanation.

claim: Targeting Lte1 to the mother cell leads to inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with misaligned spindles.
source: Targeting Lte1 to the mother cell leads to inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with misaligned spindles (Bardin et al., 2000; Bertazzi et al., 2011; Castillon et al., 2003; Geymonat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations as evidence for the zone model.

claim: Targeting Kin4 to the bud and simultaneously inactivating its inhibitor, Lte1, causes anaphase arrest even in cells with correctly positioned spindles.
source: Targeting Kin4 to the bud and simultaneously inactivating its inhibitor, Lte1, causes anaphase arrest even in cells with correctly positioned spindles (Chan and Amon, 2010; Falk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations as evidence for the zone model.

claim: The cMT - budneck model posits that MEN activity is controlled by a microtubule-based checkpoint mechanism.
source: A second model proposes that MEN activity is controlled by a microtubule-based checkpoint mechanism (Figure 1B; henceforth the 'cMT - budneck model') (Adames et al., 2001; Moore et al., 2009; Muhua et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The cMT - budneck model posits that stable contact between cytoplasmic microtubules and the bud-neck activates a checkpoint response that prevents cells from exiting mitosis.
source: The model posits that stable contact between cytoplasmic microtubules and the bud-neck activates a checkpoint response that prevents cells from exiting mitosis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the cMT - budneck model explanation.

claim: According to the cMT - budneck model, the hypothetical cMT checkpoint sensor would localize to the mother side of the septin ring.
source: The hypothetical cMT checkpoint sensor would, according to this model, localize to the mother side of the septin ring (Castillon et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cytoplasmic microtubule loss from the bud neck precedes anaphase spindle disassembly and exit from mitosis.
source: The model was proposed based on studies showing that cytoplasmic microtubule loss from the bud neck precedes anaphase spindle disassembly and exit from mitosis (Adames et al., 2001; Moore et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Laser ablation of cytoplasmic microtubules interacting with the bud neck was reported to trigger exit from mitosis.
source: Laser ablation of cytoplasmic microtubules interacting with the bud neck was further reported to trigger exit from mitosis (Moore et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: 92% of DYN1-AID kar9Δ cells initially mispositioned their spindles upon IAA addition in contrast to 13% seen in the wild type controls.
source: Live cell imaging showed that 92% of DYN1-AID kar9Δ cells initially mispositioned their spindles (i.e. had spindles greater than 2 μm in length in the mother cell compartment) upon IAA addition in contrast to 13% seen in the wild type controls.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Wild-type cells with correctly aligned spindles underwent anaphase within 19.2 ± 4.8 min.
source: Wild-type cells with correctly aligned spindles underwent anaphase within 19.2 ± 4.8 min (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E and G.

claim: DYN1-AID kar9Δ cells spent 65.9 ± 51.7 min in anaphase.
source: In contrast, DYN1-AID kar9Δ cells spent 65.9 ± 51.7 min in anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Most cells (85%) eventually were able to pull the mispositioned spindle into the bud.
source: Most cells (85%) eventually were able to pull the mispositioned spindle into the bud (see Figure 1H for an example), which was followed by exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: Only 6% of cells arrested with a mispositioned spindle for the duration of the movie analysis (longer than 200 min).
source: Only 6% of cells arrested with a mispositioned spindle for the duration of the movie analysis (longer than 200 min, open squares in Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: 9% of cells with mispositioned spindles inappropriately exited from mitosis, leading to the formation of anucleate and binucleate cells.
source: Although exit from mitosis was prevented in the majority of cells with mispositioned spindles, we observed inappropriate exit from mitosis in 9% of such cells, leading to the formation of anucleate and binucleate cells (Figure 1F and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1F and I.

claim: Cells with mispositioned spindles frequently display cMTs that contact the bud neck.
source: As reported previously, we found that cells with mispositioned spindles frequently display cMTs that contact the bud neck (Figure 2, cells 1–30; Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Video 1.

claim: In cells that exit from mitosis despite harboring a mispositioned spindle, this cell cycle transition was preceded by the loss of cMT-bud neck interactions.
source: Also consistent with previous studies, we found that in cells that exit from mitosis despite harboring a mispositioned spindle, this cell cycle transition was preceded by the loss of cMT-bud neck interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Contact between cMTs and the bud neck was lost approximately 2–8 min before spindle breakdown in cells that exit from mitosis despite harboring a mispositioned spindle.
source: Contact was lost approximately 2–8 min before spindle breakdown (Figure 2, cells 31–37; Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: The majority of cells with mispositioned spindles lacked cMT-bud neck contacts for significant periods of time yet stayed arrested in anaphase.
source: Importantly, our analysis also revealed that inappropriate mitotic exit was not an obligatory consequence of loss of cMT – bud neck interactions. The majority of cells with mispositioned spindles lacked cMT-bud neck contacts for significant periods of time yet stayed arrested in anaphase (Video 4; Figure 2, cells 1–30).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Video 4.

claim: Loss of cMT – bud neck interactions does not necessarily cause inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles.
source: We conclude that loss of cMT – bud neck interactions does not necessarily cause inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: Ablation of cMTs does not promote exit from mitosis in the vast majority (33/35) of cells analyzed.
source: In summary, our results show that ablation of cMTs does not promote exit from mitosis in the vast majority (33/35) of cells analyzed (Figure 3C, mispositioned spindles category).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Although cMT retraction frequently precedes inappropriate exit from mitosis in cells with misaligned spindles, it is not the cause of exit from mitosis in these cells.
source: We conclude that although cMT retraction frequently precedes inappropriate exit from mitosis in cells with misaligned spindles, it is not the cause of exit from mitosis in these cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Cdc14 release from the nucleolus preceded both, cMT retraction from the bud neck and mitotic spindle breakdown in cells that exited mitosis despite harboring a misaligned spindle.
source: Live cell imaging showed that Cdc14 release from the nucleolus preceded both, cMT retraction from the bud neck and mitotic spindle breakdown in cells that exited mitosis despite harboring a misaligned spindle.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: In 78.22 ± 3.0% of cells, Cdc14 release occurred approximately 5 min prior to loss of cMT – bud neck interactions and approximately 5–15 min prior to mitotic spindle breakdown.
source: In 78.22 ± 3.0% of cells (n ≥ 37 cells per biological replicate. 3 replicates were performed), Cdc14 release occurred approximately 5 min prior to loss of cMT – bud neck interactions and approximately 5–15 min prior to mitotic spindle breakdown (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the majority of cells (73.85 ± 4.4%) Cdc14 release from the nucleolus occurred during anaphase.
source: In the majority of cells (73.85 ± 4.4%) Cdc14 release from the nucleolus occurred during anaphase (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In a small fraction of cells (4.4 ± 4.1%), Cdc14 appeared to be fully released already at the metaphase to anaphase transition.
source: However in a small fraction of these cells, 4.4 ± 4.1%, Cdc14 appeared to be fully released already at the metaphase to anaphase transition (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The coefficient of variation of Cdc14-td Tomato pixel intensity decreased before cMT retraction from the bud neck.
source: Despite this limitation, it was nevertheless clear that the coefficient of variation of Cdc14-td Tomato pixel intensity decreased before cMT retraction from the bud neck (Figure 4B,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4B, D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In 10.8 ± 4.9% of cells Cdc14 release from the nucleolus occurred concomitantly with cMT retraction.
source: Not all cells showed release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus prior to cMT retraction from the bud neck. In 10.8 ± 4.9% of cells Cdc14 release from the nucleolus occurred concomitantly with cMT retraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Cdc14 release never occurred after cMT retraction from the bud neck.
source: Importantly, we never observed that Cdc14 release occurred after cMT retraction from the bud neck.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the data analysis.

claim: Depletion of Cdc14 suppressed exit from mitosis in the rare wild-type cells that escape the anaphase arrest when their spindles are mispositioned.
source: Consistent with the idea that Cdc14 triggers inappropriate exit from mitosis in cells with mispositioned spindles we find that depletion of Cdc14 suppressed exit from mitosis in the rare wild-type cells that escape the anaphase arrest when their spindles are mispositioned (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles is not due to loss of cMT – bud neck interactions.
source: We conclude that inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles is not due to loss of cMT – bud neck interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: cMT retraction is a consequence of Cdc14 release from the nucleolus in cells with mispositioned spindles that exit from mitosis.
source: Rather, cMT retraction is a consequence of Cdc14 release from the nucleolus in these cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the data in Figure 4.

claim: The reason why loss of cMT – bud neck interactions always precedes mitotic spindle breakdown in cells with mispositioned spindles that exit from mitosis is because disassembly of a single cMT occurs more quickly than disassembly of the mitotic spindle.
source: We further propose that the reason why loss of cMT – bud neck interactions always precedes mitotic spindle breakdown in cells with mispositioned spindles that exit from mitosis is because disassembly of a single cMT occurs more quickly than disassembly of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is a proposal stated in the Results section based on the data analysis.

claim: Inhibition of the MEN suppressed the inappropriate mitotic exit that is observed in the 11% of cells that exit from mitosis when their spindle is mispositioned.
source: Not surprisingly, inhibition of the MEN, a pathway which is essential for exit from mitosis in all cells, suppressed the inappropriate mitotic exit that is observed in the 11% of cells that exit from mitosis when their spindle is mispositioned (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Inactivation of the FEAR network, either by deleting SPO12 or SLK19, prevented the inappropriate exit from mitosis in cells with mispositioned spindles.
source: We were, however, surprised to find that inactivation of the FEAR network, either by deleting SPO12 or SLK19 also prevented the inappropriate exit from mitosis in cells with mispositioned spindles (Figure 5C) (Scarfone et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Deleting SPO12 largely did not affect cMT-bud neck interactions despite completely suppressing inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles.
source: Consistent with the idea that cMT – bud neck interactions are not regulating mitotic exit, we found that deleting SPO12 largely did not affect these interactions (compare Figures 2 and 5E) despite completely suppressing inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figures 2 and 5E.

claim: In cells with mispositioned spindles, the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus was prevented in cells lacking SPO12.
source: Finally, in cells with mispositioned spindles, we found that the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus was prevented in cells lacking SPO12 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: cMT – bud neck interactions are not responsible for preventing Cdc14 activation and exit from mitosis in response to mispositioned spindles.
source: Together, our data lead to the following two conclusions. First, cMT – bud neck interactions are not responsible for preventing Cdc14 activation and exit from mitosis in response to mispositioned spindles.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the data in Figures 2-5.

claim: Activation of Cdc14 causes cMT retraction from the bud neck and exit from mitosis in cells with mispositioned spindles that inappropriately exit from mitosis.
source: Instead, activation of Cdc14 causes cMT retraction from the bud neck and exit from mitosis in cells with mispositioned spindles that inappropriately exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Cdc14 activation in the cells that exit from mitosis despite harboring a mispositioned spindle depends on the FEAR network.
source: Second, Cdc14 activation in the cells that exit from mitosis despite harboring a mispositioned spindle depends on the FEAR network.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the data in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: It is high FEAR network activity that causes bypass of the anaphase arrest triggered by spindle misposition in some cells.
source: This observation raises the interesting possibility that it is high FEAR network activity that causes bypass of the anaphase arrest triggered by spindle misposition in some cells.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Results section based on the data in Figure 5.

claim: In Class I cells (both spindles correctly aligned), both spindles entered the bud in quick sequence during anaphase and exit from mitosis occurred promptly thereafter.
source: In cells in which both spindles were correctly aligned along the mother – bud axis (Class I cells) both spindles entered the bud in quick sequence during anaphase and exit from mitosis (as judged by Cdc3 loss from the bud neck) occurred promptly thereafter (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: Class II cells exited mitosis even though only one spindle entered the bud during anaphase.
source: Class II cells also exited mitosis even though only one spindle entered the bud during anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: Average anaphase duration for Class II cells was 15.7 ± 2.3 min, which was comparable to the average anaphase duration in cells in which both spindles were correctly positioned (16.6 ± 3.7 min).
source: Average anaphase duration for these cells was 15.7 ± 2.3 min, which was comparable to the average anaphase duration in cells in which both spindles were correctly positioned (16.6 ± 3.7 min; compare Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The time of entry of one spindle into the bud until exit from mitosis was the same in cells in which both spindles aligned correctly and cells in which one spindle was correctly aligned and the other was misaligned.
source: Furthermore the time of entry of one spindle into the bud until exit from mitosis was the same in cells in which both spindles aligned correctly and cells in which one spindle was correctly aligned and the other was misaligned (compare Figure 6C,D column 'bud entry to exit from mitosis').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6C and D.

claim: In the vast majority of Class II delayed cells (42/51 cells), it was only once one spindle moved from the mother compartment into the bud that cells promptly exited mitosis.
source: In the vast majority of these cells it was only once one spindle moved from the mother compartment into the bud that cells promptly exited mitosis (42/51 cells).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: Six cells (11.76%) permanently arrested in anaphase with both spindles in the mother cell compartment.
source: Of the remaining cells, six cells (11.76%) permanently arrested in anaphase with both spindles in the mother cell compartment
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: Two cells inappropriately exited mitosis with both spindles in the mother cell (3.92%).
source: and two inappropriately exited mitosis with both spindles in the mother cell (3.92%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: In a very small fraction of cells (1/51), exit from mitosis occurred even when the mispositioned spindle in the mother cell had not yet initiated anaphase.
source: Strikingly, we also noticed that in a very small fraction of cells (1/51), exit from mitosis occurred even when the mispositioned spindle in the mother cell had not yet initiated anaphase (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Movement of one spindle pole into the bud triggers exit from mitosis.
source: We conclude that movement of one spindle pole into the bud triggers exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the heterokaryon data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: In cells that harbor one nucleus in the bud and one in the mother cell, both spindles are mispositioned, yet exit from mitosis occurs once the spindle in the bud has initiated anaphase.
source: In cells that harbor one nucleus in the bud and one in the mother cell, both spindles are mispositioned, yet exit from mitosis occurs once the spindle in the bud has initiated anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the analysis of Class III cells in Figure 8D.

claim: Exit from mitosis is not triggered by a correctly positioned spindle but rather a spindle that is in the bud.
source: This result indicates that exit from mitosis is not triggered by a correctly positioned spindle but rather a spindle that is in the bud, as exit from mitosis occurred in class III cells even though the spindle in the bud was mispositioned.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the analysis of Class III cells in Figure 8D.

claim: A spindle simply being in the bud is not sufficient to bring about exit from mitosis; exit from mitosis only occurred after the bud-localized spindle had undergone anaphase.
source: It is important to note however, that a spindle simply being in the bud is not sufficient to bring about exit from mitosis. Exit from mitosis only occurred after the bud-localized spindle had undergone anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the analysis of heterokaryon data.

claim: Anaphase entry is required for MEN activation and exit from mitosis.
source: This observation is consistent with previous findings showing that anaphase entry is required for MEN activation and exit from mitosis (Rock and Amon, 2011) (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The heterokaryon analyses do not support the hypothesis that a dominant inhibitory signal originating from a mispositioned spindle prevents MEN activation and exit from mitosis.
source: In summary, our heterokaryon analyses do not support the hypothesis that a dominant inhibitory signal originating from a mispositioned spindle prevents MEN activation and exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the heterokaryon data in Figures 6-8.

claim: Movement of the spindle into the bud as occurs during a cell cycle with a correctly positioned spindle activates the MEN and exit from mitosis.
source: Instead, our data show that movement of the spindle into the bud as occurs during a cell cycle with a correctly positioned spindle activates the MEN and exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the heterokaryon data in Figures 6-8.

claim: The site of cytokinesis in budding yeast is determined long before cells undergo mitosis.
source: In budding yeast, the site of cytokinesis is determined long before cells undergo mitosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Division by budding requires sophisticated mechanisms to position the nucleus along the mother – bud axis.
source: Therefore division by budding not only requires sophisticated mechanisms to position the nucleus along the mother – bud axis, it also requires mechanisms to prevent cells from exiting mitosis and undergoing cytokinesis until the nuclei are partitioned between the mother and bud cell compartments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: In 1995, Yeh et al. demonstrated that cells with mispositioned spindles arrest in late anaphase and fail to exit from mitosis.
source: In 1995, Yeh et al. demonstrated the existence of such a mechanism. They showed that cells with mispositioned spindles arrest in late anaphase and fail to exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Muhua et al. (1998) termed the regulatory mechanism that prevents exit from mitosis in cells with misaligned spindles the spindle position checkpoint (SPoC).
source: Subsequently, Muhua et al. (1998) termed this regulatory mechanism the spindle position checkpoint (SPoC).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Exit from mitosis is prevented in cells with misaligned spindles through the inhibition of the Mitotic Exit Network.
source: Ensuing studies showed that exit from mitosis is prevented in cells with misaligned spindles through the inhibition of the Mitotic Exit Network, the GTPase signaling cascade that promotes anaphase spindle disassembly, chromosome decondensation and cytokinesis by activating Cdc14 (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The data support the conclusion that a correctly aligned spindle promotes exit from mitosis.
source: Our data support the conclusion that a correctly aligned spindle promotes exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: It is the movement of the MEN component-carrying SPB into the bud that signals exit from mitosis.
source: Our data, together with previous studies, further indicate that it is the movement of the MEN component-carrying SPB into the bud that signals exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings and previous studies.

claim: Retraction of cMTs occurs frequently and often for extended periods of time also in cells with-mispositioned spindles that do not inappropriately exit mitosis in the mother cell compartment.
source: First, retraction of cMTs occurs frequently and often for extended periods of time also in cells with-mispositioned spindles that do not inappropriately exit mitosis in the mother cell compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: In the cMT ablation studies, exit from mitosis was not observed following the loss of cMT – bud neck interactions.
source: Second, in our cMT ablation studies we did not observe exit from mitosis following the loss of cMT – bud neck interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: Not all mutants that lack cytoplasmic microtubules exhibit an increased frequency in inappropriate exit from mitosis when the spindle is mispositioned.
source: Third, not all mutants that lack cytoplasmic microtubules exhibit an increased frequency in inappropriate exit from mitosis when the spindle is mispositioned.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a reference to an accompanying paper.

claim: Gryaznova et al. found that cells lacking SPC72 arrest in anaphase when their spindles are mispositioned despite the absence of cMTs.
source: Gryaznova et al. (accompanying paper) found that cells lacking SPC72 arrest in anaphase when their spindles are mispositioned despite the absence of cMTs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a reference to an accompanying paper.

claim: cMT retraction from the bud neck did not precede Cdc14 release from the nucleolus but was a consequence thereof.
source: The most conclusive demonstration that loss of cMT bud neck interactions does not trigger exit from mitosis was the analysis of Cdc14 localization. It clearly showed that cMT retraction from the bud neck did not precede Cdc14 release from the nucleolus but was a consequence thereof.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 4.

claim: The reason why cMTs invariably disassemble prior to the mitotic spindle in cells that exit mitosis with mispositioned spindles is that disassembly of a single cMT upon mitotic CDK inactivation takes less time than the disassembly of a mitotic spindle that is composed of many microtubules.
source: We propose that the reason why cMTs invariably disassemble prior to the mitotic spindle in such cells is that disassembly of a single cMT upon mitotic CDK inactivation takes less time than the disassembly of a mitotic spindle that is composed of many microtubules.
evidence: This is a proposal stated in the Discussion section based on the data analysis.

claim: MEN signaling takes place at SPBs.
source: MEN signaling takes place at SPBs (Maekawa et al., 2007; Valerio-Santiago and Monje-Casas, 2011; Visintin and Amon, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The GTPase Tem1 and Polo kinase recruit the MEN kinase Cdc15 to SPBs where it is activated by an unknown mechanism.
source: The GTPase Tem1 and Polo kinase recruit the MEN kinase Cdc15 to SPBs where it is activated by an unknown mechanism (Rock and Amon, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Regulators of the GTPase Tem1 are strategically placed in the cell: Kin4 localizes to the mother cell, Lte1 localizes to the bud.
source: Regulators of the GTPase are strategically placed in the cell. Kin4, the GTPase inhibitor localizes to the mother cell, the Kin4 inhibitor and hence MEN activator Lte1 localizes to the bud (Bardin et al., 2000; D'Aquino et al., 2005; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: When both of the spindle pole bodies are in the MEN inhibitory mother cell compartment, the cell cannot exit from mitosis and arrests in anaphase.
source: When both of the spindle pole bodies are in the MEN inhibitory mother cell compartment, the cell cannot exit from mitosis and arrests in anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the zone model explanation.

claim: It is only once one MEN component-bearing spindle pole body moves into the mitotic exit-activating zone in the bud does the MEN become active and exit from mitosis occurs.
source: It is only once one MEN component-bearing spindle pole body moves into the mitotic exit-activating zone in the bud does the MEN become active and exit from mitosis occurs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the zone model explanation.

claim: The zone model takes into account that not only are there MEN inhibiting factors in the mother cell compartment, but that there are also factors in the bud that promote exit from mitosis.
source: It is important to emphasize that the zone model takes into account that not only are there MEN inhibiting factors in the mother cell compartment, but that there are also factors in the bud that promote exit from mitosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Irrespective of whether or not a cell harbors a mispositioned spindle, exit from mitosis occurs once one anaphase spindle enters the bud.
source: Irrespective of whether or not a cell harbors a mispositioned spindle, exit from mitosis occurs once one anaphase spindle enters the bud.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the heterokaryon data.

claim: It is the presence of a spindle pole in bud and not a correctly positioned spindle that leads to MEN activation.
source: Our analysis of heterokaryons in which one of the two spindles gets pulled into the bud in its entirety further shows that it is the presence of a spindle pole in bud and not a correctly positioned spindle that leads to MEN activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the analysis of Class III cells.

claim: In cells that harbor one nucleus in the bud and one in the mother cell, both spindles are mispositioned, yet exit from mitosis occurs once the spindle in the bud has initiated anaphase.
source: In cells that harbor one nucleus in the bud and one in the mother cell, both spindles are mispositioned, yet exit from mitosis occurs once the spindle in the bud has initiated anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the analysis of Class III cells.

claim: Two signals are necessary for MEN activation in anaphase: (1) a spatial signal – the movement of a MEN bearing SPB into the bud and (2) a temporal signal that indicates that anaphase chromosome segregation has occurred.
source: This finding further demonstrates that two signals are necessary for MEN activation in anaphase: (1) a spatial signal – the movement of a MEN bearing SPB into the bud and (2) a temporal signal that indicates that anaphase chromosome segregation has occurred (Bardin et al., 2000; Chan and Amon, 2010; Manzoni et al., 2010; Rock and Amon, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: A small fraction of cells exit from mitosis despite the presence of a mispositioned spindle.
source: It has long been known that a small fraction of cells exit from mitosis despite the presence of a mispositioned spindle (Adames et al., 2001; D'Aquino et al., 2005; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles is preceded by the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus.
source: We show here that this event is preceded by the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 4.

claim: Cdc14 activation in cells with mispositioned spindles that inappropriately exit from mitosis requires FEAR network function.
source: Our data further indicate that this Cdc14 activation requires FEAR network function because inappropriate mitotic exit in cells with mispositioned spindles is completely prevented when FEAR network component encoding genes are deleted.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figure 5C.

claim: FEAR network activity is under the control of the regulatory mechanisms governing the metaphase – anaphase transition.
source: FEAR network activity is under the control of the regulatory mechanisms governing the metaphase – anaphase transition (Stegmeier et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) inhibits entry into anaphase until all chromosomes have attached correctly to the mitotic spindle.
source: At this cell cycle transition, a checkpoint known as the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) inhibits entry into anaphase until all chromosomes have attached correctly to the mitotic spindle (reviewed in Musacchio and Salmon (2007)).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Once the SAC is satisfied, the SAC inhibition of Separase is alleviated and the protease initiates chromosome segregation by cleaving cohesins.
source: Once this has occurred, the SAC inhibition of a protease known as Separase is alleviated and the protease initiates chromosome segregation by cleaving cohesins, the protein complexes that hold sister chromatids together (Nasmyth, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Separase is a component of the FEAR network.
source: As Separase is also a component of the FEAR network (Stegmeier et al., 2002), SAC activity also governs the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus during early anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: SAC activity governs the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus during early anaphase.
source: As Separase is also a component of the FEAR network (Stegmeier et al., 2002), SAC activity also governs the release of Cdc14 from the nucleolus during early anaphase.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The data are inconsistent with a model where cMT-bud-neck interactions prevent exit from mitosis in cells with mispositioned spindles.
source: Our data are inconsistent with a model where cMT-bud-neck interactions prevent exit from mitosis in cells with mispositioned spindles.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Spatial regulation of the MEN is controlled through the delivery of a MEN component bearing SPB into the bud.
source: Instead, they support the conclusion that spatial regulation of the MEN is controlled through the delivery of a MEN component bearing SPB into the bud.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Checkpoint regulation has been described for other asymmetric divisions.
source: Checkpoint regulation has been described for other asymmetric divisions (Cheng et al., 2008; O'Connell and Wang, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: In Drosophila male germline stem cells with mispositioned centrosomes, cell cycle progression is delayed until the centrosomes properly align with respect to the mother-daughter axis of division.
source: In Drosophila male germline stem cells with mispositioned centrosomes, cell cycle progression is delayed until the centrosomes properly align with respect to the mother-daughter axis of division (Cheng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The AMP-related kinase family member Par-1 (of which Kin4 is also a member) has been shown to be important in delaying cell cycle progression in response to mispositioned spindles in male germline stem cells.
source: Additionally, the AMP-related kinase family member Par-1 (of which Kin4 is also a member) has been shown to be important in delaying cell cycle progression in response to mispositioned spindles in male germline stem cells (Pereira and Yamashita, 2011; Yuan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.
